# PL/SQL Exception Handling

PL/SQL reports failure by raising, not by returning. That single fact reshapes how blocks are written,
because the most common statement in the language — `SELECT INTO` — has **three** outcomes and only
one of them is a value.

## `SELECT INTO` is all-or-nothing

> "SELECT INTO is all-or-nothing. Exactly one row satisfies it; zero rows raise NO_DATA_FOUND and two
> or more raise TOO_MANY_ROWS. Both are exceptions, not return values, so every block below that uses
> it handles them explicitly."
> — Oracle-Database-Laboratories/sql/03_plsql/01_blocks_and_exceptions.sql, 2026-07-25

A consequence that bites: **when `SELECT INTO` raises, its `INTO` target is left unassigned.** The
lookup block in [[oracle-database-laboratories]] therefore prints the *searched-for* variable in its
handlers, not the target — reporting the target would print an empty string exactly where the
diagnostic is needed. Handlers must read from state that was valid before the failure.

## Three sources of exception

| Source | Example here |
|---|---|
| **Predefined** | `NO_DATA_FOUND`, `TOO_MANY_ROWS` around `SELECT INTO` |
| **User-defined** | `already_exists`, `invalid_band_no` — declared `EXCEPTION`, raised by `RAISE`, caught by name |
| **`SQLCODE` inspection** | the teardown script catches `WHEN OTHERS`, allows ORA-00942 and ORA-04043, re-raises everything else |

The third pattern is worth isolating. A bare `WHEN OTHERS THEN NULL` swallows everything and is the
single most damaging idiom in the language. The teardown script's version tests `SQLCODE IN (-942,
-4043)` and calls `RAISE` in the `ELSE` — so "the object was already gone" is tolerated and a genuine
failure still propagates. That narrow, deliberate swallow is what makes
[[idempotent-teardown-scripts]] safe rather than reckless.

## Reporting failure across a boundary

A stored procedure that catches its own exception and prints a message returns normally, leaving the
caller unable to distinguish success from rejection. `herd_admin.add_band` instead raises through
`RAISE_APPLICATION_ERROR` in the **-20000 to -20999** range Oracle reserves for application errors —
any other code produces ORA-21000 in place of the intended message. See [[plsql]].

The caller's side of the same contract is visible in the exercise loop: each call is wrapped in its
own inner `BEGIN … EXCEPTION WHEN OTHERS THEN` that prints `SQLERRM` and continues, so one rejection
does not abort the batch. Raise at the boundary, decide at the call site.

## Two failures that look like a working handler

Both are recorded in the same file, and both produce a *wrong answer* rather than an error:

- **Name collision.** Where a PL/SQL variable or parameter shares a name with a column, PL/SQL
  resolves in favour of the PL/SQL identifier. `WHERE name = name_band` becomes a tautology, the
  duplicate check silently passes on everything, and nothing raises. The fix is to qualify every
  predicate with the table name. The procedure version in `03_procedures_and_packages.sql` documents
  exactly this collision at the point where it would occur.
- **Buffer overflow inside the handler.** The clash-message buffer is `VARCHAR2(200)`, not 50,
  because three appended clashes overflow a 50-character buffer and ORA-06502 replaces the diagnostic
  the handler existed to produce. A handler that can itself raise is not a handler.

Both are instances of [[tests-that-pass-for-the-wrong-reason]] expressed in a language with no tests —
the check runs, reports success, and checks nothing.
